title: switch and case
learningGoals: write a switch with case labels

youtube.title: C++ switch Statement: Menus Made Easy | C++ Programming EP 15
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a switch with case labels, use break to end each case and add a default case, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 switch and case · 1:21 Name the day · 2:20 Jump to the case · 3:05 Second program · 4:15 Recap · 4:45 Bug of the Day · 5:43 Challenge · 6:08 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a menu board with numbered dishes

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we build a menu with switch. It is a neat way to pick one action from many.

scenes.onScreen: "switch and case": numbered lines (1. Switch jumps to the matching case; 2. Break ends the case; 3. Default handles all other values) and an analogy card: a restaurant menu: you say a number and the kitchen makes that dish
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A switch statement compares one value with many case labels. It jumps to the matching case. The break keyword ends that case. The default case handles all other values. Without break, the program falls through into the next case. Think of a menu board. You say a number, and the kitchen makes that dish. Use a switch when you compare one value with many fixed choices. The code is shorter than a long ladder, and it is easier to read. But a switch works only with whole numbers and characters. It cannot compare text or decimals. The break keyword is the most important part. Without it, the program keeps running into the next case.
points: Switch jumps to the matching case

analogy.title: switch and case
analogy.body: A restaurant menu: you say a number and the kitchen makes that dish

scenes.onScreen: day.cpp: a switch turns a number into a day name
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Day is three. [HL 6] The switch looks at the value of day. [HL 7] Case one does not match. [HL 8] Case two does not match. [HL 9] Case three matches, so the program prints Wednesday. Then break leaves the switch. [HL 10] The default case runs when no case matches. [HL 6] The switch looks at day only once. Then it jumps straight to the right label. [HL 9] A match prints Wednesday. The break on the same line jumps out of the switch. [HL 10] The default case is last. It has no break, because nothing follows it. Always write a default case. It tells the reader that you thought about the other values.

scenes.onScreen: a table: value, case and output
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: The table shows how the switch picks a case. The value of day finds the matching row. If no row matches, the default row runs. Case labels must be whole numbers or characters, not text. Notice that the table has one row for each label. The switch reads the value, finds its row, and runs the code from that row down to the first break. That last part is the key. Remember it when you see fall-through.

diagram.caption: a table: value, case and output

scenes.onScreen: menu.cpp: a switch on a character with a shared case
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The choice is the letter b. [HL 7] Two case labels can share one action. Here the letters a and A both add. [HL 11] Our letter b matches this case. [HL 13] It prints Buy. [HL 14] Break then ends the switch. [HL 15] Default would handle any other letter. [HL 7] A case label with no code under it falls through on purpose. Two letters share one action. This is the one time when missing break is useful. [HL 13] Add a comment when you do this, so the next reader knows it is on purpose.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as menu dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Buy. Try the capital letter B as well. It must print Buy too.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Switch compares one value with many cases. Two. Break ends a case. Three. Default handles all other values. Four. Two cases can share one action. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Switch compares one value with many cases.
Two cases can share one action.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A missing break
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. Case three has no break. The program prints Wednesday, and then Thursday too. It falls through into the next case, and the compiler warns about it. Without a break, the switch does not stop. Add break at the end of each case. Fall-through is a feature, but it surprises beginners. The program runs every line from the matching case until it finds a break. Turn on warnings with the Wall flag, and the compiler tells you when a break is missing.

scenes.onScreen: I asked the switch for a table at the restaurant. It gave me two, because I forgot the break.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I asked the switch for a table at the restaurant. It gave me two, because I forgot the break.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make a calculator menu
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Use a switch on a character. For plus, minus and times, print the result of seven and three. Hint: use the char type for the choice, and print one result in each case. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: while loops. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

day.cpp: In function 'int main()':
day.cpp:7:40: warning: this statement may fall through [-Wimplicit-fallthrough=]
    7 |         case 3: cout << "Wednesday" << endl;
      |                                        ^~~~
day.cpp:8:9: note: here
    8 |         case 4: cout << "Thursday" << endl; break;
bug.why: Without break, the program keeps running into the next case. This is called fall-through.

challenge: Use a switch on a character. For plus, minus and times, print the result of seven and three. Hint: use the char type for the choice, and print one result in each case.
challengeAnswer: Use case with single quotes for each sign. Print seven plus three, seven minus three and seven times three, and add break after each.
